chunks: My father and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn al-Walid (may God be pleased with them) narrated to us, saying: Sa'd narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr al-Bizanti, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him)
He said: I said to him, 'Some of our companions say by al-Jabr (compulsion/determinism) and some say by al-Isita'ah (free will/capacity).'

God, the Blessed and Exalted, said: 'O son of Adam! By your will you are the one who wills for yourself whatever you will, and by My power you have carried out My prescribed duties for Me, and by My bounty you have become strong in disobeying Me. I made you hearing, seeing, and strong.'

Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself. And that is because I am more worthy of your good deeds than you are, and you are more worthy of your evil deeds than I am.
And that is because I am not questioned for what I do, but they are questioned.
So I have strung together for you everything you desire.
ai.seo_question: How does Shia theology reconcile divine decree (al-Jabr) with human free will (al-Isita'ah)?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Rida (AS) in *Uyun Akhbar al-Rida* offers a nuanced Shia resolution to the Jabr (determinism) vs. Ikhtiyar (free will) debate by synthesizing divine omnipotence with human responsibility. It clarifies that while God’s will and power are the ultimate source of existence and capability, humans are the primary agents of their choices, making them more deserving of credit for good deeds and blame for sins. This 'position between the two positions' (Bayn al-Amrayn) underscores that God is not the author of evil, preserving both His justice and human accountability.
